en: Thus have I heard: [Majjhima Nikāya 98, the Vāseṭṭha Sutta]
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove.
Now at that time many well-known and highly distinguished brahmin householders were residing at Icchānaṅgala, namely:
the brahmin Caṅkī, the brahmin Tārukkha, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, the brahmin Todeyya, and other well-known and highly distinguished brahmin householders.
Then, as the young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja were walking and wandering for exercise, this discussion arose between them:
"How, sir, does one become a brahmin?
The young brahmin Bhāradvāja spoke thus:
“But, sir, when one is well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and irreproachable with respect to birth—
to that extent, sir, one is a brahmin.
Thus spoke the young man Vāseṭṭha.
“But when, sir, he is virtuous and perfect in his conduct—
it is by this much, sir, that one becomes a brahmin.
Neither was the young Brahmin Bhāradvāja able to convince the young Brahmin Vāseṭṭha, nor was the young Brahmin Vāseṭṭha able to convince the young Brahmin Bhāradvāja.
Then the young Brahmin Vāseṭṭha addressed the young Brahmin Bhāradvāja:
"Sir Bhāradvāja, this ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is staying at Icchānaṅgala in the grove of Icchānaṅgala.
A fine report concerning the venerable Gotama has spread abroad thus:"

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Come, Master Bhāradvāja, let us approach the ascetic Gotama; having approached, we will ask the ascetic Gotama about this matter.
We shall bear it in mind exactly as the ascetic Gotama explains it to us.”
“Yes, sir,” the young brahmin Bhāradvāja replied to the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha.
Then the young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha addressed the Blessed One in verses:
“We both claim to be authorized and recognized as possessors of the threefold knowledge.”
I am Pokkharasāti,
and this young brahmin is Tārukkha;
[we are those] who have declared what is taught by the possessors of the threefold knowledge.
In that regard, we are solitary ones (kevalin);
we are etymologists of words and like masters in recitation.
Regarding this doctrine of birth,
O Gotama, there is a dispute among us:
"One becomes a brahmin by birth."
"Bhāradvāja" is how he is called;
but I call him by his action—
know this, O Seer.
We two were unable to inform one another;
we have come to question you, sir.
Renowned as the Perfectly Awakened One—
just as people, having approached the moon that has passed beyond waning, stand with palms joined in reverence; so too do they honor him.
In this world, they pay homage and revere Gotama,
the Eye that has arisen in the world.
We ask Gotama this:
Is one a brahmin by birth,
or does one become so through action?
“Tell us who do not know,
so that we may come to know a brahmin.
“I shall explain this to you,” he said.
"Vāseṭṭha," said the Blessed One,
"I shall explain to you in due order and according to reality the classification of living beings by birth."
Know that there are various species even among grasses and trees,
though they do not claim such status for themselves.
Their gender is determined by birth,
for their births are distinct from one another;
then [there are] insects and moths.
Down to the ant and the dung-beetle;
their characteristic is composed of birth,
for their births are indeed distinct from one another.
Know also the four-footed creatures,
both small and large;
their gender is innate.
For species are indeed diverse from one another.
Know them also among those with bellies for feet,
the serpents with long backs.
Their gender consists of birth,
for their births are distinct from one another;
therefore, know them even among the fish.
In water dwell those whose range is the water;
their gender is determined by birth,
for their births are indeed distinct from one another.
From that you should also know the birds that travel through the air on their wings;
their characteristic mark consists of their birth.
For the classes of beings are distinct from one another.
Just as among these classes,
the gender is diverse and inherent in each class;
Thus, among humans,
there is no distinct mark consisting of birth;
neither by the hair nor by the head [is it known].
Not with the ears, nor with the eyes;
not with the mouth, nor with the nose,
nor with the lips or the eyebrows.
Not with the neck, nor with the shoulders,
not with the belly, nor with the back;
not with the hips, nor with the chest.
Not in a confined place, nor during sexual intercourse;
not with hands, nor with feet,
nor with fingers, nor with nails.
Neither by the calves nor by the thighs,
nor by complexion or voice,
is there any mark consisting of birth.
Just as it is in other births,
so too within one's own bodies—
this is not found among human beings.
And among humans, it is called by the conventional designation "personality-factors" (vokāra).
For whoever among humans...
He lives off the protection of cattle;
know this, Vāseṭṭha:
he is a farmer, not a brahmin.
Whoever among humans lives by various crafts—
know this, Vāseṭṭha, to be so.
He is an artisan, not a brahmin.
For whoever among human beings lives by trade, [is an artisan].
Know this, Vāseṭṭha:
whoever among men is such a person is a merchant, not a brahmin.
For whoever [is thus] among men...
He lives by means of another's service;
know this, Vāseṭṭha,
he is a servant, not a brahmin.
"Whoever among humans lives off what has not been given—
know this, Vāseṭṭha, to be so."
This is a thief, not a brahmin.
For whoever among human beings lives by the profession of arms;
"Know this, Vāseṭṭha:
one who is a warrior among men is not a brahmin."
He lives by means of priesthood;
know this, Vāseṭṭha:
he is a sacrificer, not a brahmin.
Whoever among humans enjoys a village or a kingdom—
know this, Vāseṭṭha, to be so.
"This man is a king, not a brahmin.
And I do not call one a brahmin by birth from a womb or by descent from a mother."
He is called a "mere talker" if he possesses anything;
but one who has nothing and grasps at nothing—
Him I call a brahmin: he who,
having severed all fetters,
indeed does not tremble.
One who has transcended attachment and is detached from the fetters— him I call a brahmin.
Having cut through the thong and the strap,
Who has cut the bond along with its tendency,
who has lifted the crossbar— the Buddha—
I call him a brahmin.
He who, free from malice, endures abuse, execution, and imprisonment—
his strength is the army of patience.
Him I call a brahmin:
one who is free from anger, steadfast in his vows,
virtuous, and free from pride.
One who is tamed, in his final body—
him I call a brahmin.
Like water on a lotus leaf...
Like a mustard seed on the point of an awl,
he who is not smeared by sensual pleasures—
him I call a brahmin.
He who understands suffering and its very exhaustion right here in this world— him,
whose burden is laid down and who is disjoined from bonds, I call a brahmin.
Him I call a brahmin—
one of profound wisdom, possessed of intelligence,
and skilled in discerning the path from the non-path.
One who has attained the highest goal—
him I call a brahmin. One who does not associate with householders...
Free from both [home and homelessness],
wandering without a fixed abode, and possessing few desires—
him I call a brahmin.
Having laid aside the rod toward all beings,
both those that are frail and those that are firm,
he who neither kills nor causes others to kill—
Him I call a brahmin: one who is unprovoked among those who provoke,
and who has attained peace amidst those who wield the rod of violence.
Among those who grasp, he who is without grasping—
him I call a brahmin.
He for whom both lust and hatred...
Conceit and hypocrisy are laid aside like a mustard seed from the point of an awl;
him I call a brahmin.
One should utter speech that is not harsh, informative, true,
and by which one does not provoke anyone.
Him I call a brahmin:
whoever [abstains from] taking long or short,
fine or coarse, pleasant or unpleasant—
In this world, he takes nothing that is not given;
him I call a brahmin.
He in whom no desires exist—
In this world and in the next,
free from longing and detached—
that one I call a brahmin.
For whom no underlying tendencies exist,
who through final knowledge is free from doubt,
and who has reached the immersion in the Deathless—
Him I call a brahmin:
he who has overcome both merit and evil,
having transcended both attachments.
One who is sorrowless, stainless, and pure—
him I call a brahmin.
Like the moon, spotless and pure.
Serene and untroubled,
with the destruction of delight and becoming—
him I call a brahmin.
He who has transcended this quagmire, this difficult path,
this delusion of saṃsāra—
he is a meditator who has crossed over and reached the further shore.
Unshaken, free from doubt,
extinguished through non-clinging—
him I call a brahmin.
Having abandoned sensual desires,
one should wander as a homeless renunciant,
with craving for sense-pleasures and existence utterly destroyed.
Him I call a brahmin: he who,
having abandoned craving,
wanders as a homeless renunciant.
One whose craving and becoming are utterly exhausted— him I call a brahmin.
Having abandoned human bondage,
He has transcended divine bonds;
one who is detached from all bonds— him I call a brahmin.
Having abandoned both delight and aversion,
become cooled and free from acquisitions—
the Hero who has overcome the entire world—
Him I call a brahmin:
he who fully understands the passing away of beings and their rebirth in every way.
One who is unattached, well-gone, and awakened—
him I call a brahmin.
Whose destination they do not know,
Gods, gandhabbas, and humans—
him who has destroyed the taints, the Arahant,
him I call a brahmin.
For one who has nothing before, after,
or in between; who is without possessions and without grasping—
Him I call a brahmin:
a bull, a preeminent hero,
a great seer, a victor.
The one who is unmoving, washed clean, awakened—
him I call a brahmin.
He who knows his former abodes...
He sees both heaven and the states of woe;
having reached the destruction of birth—
him I call a brahmin.
For this is merely a conventional designation in the world,
a name and clan established by convention,
arisen from a collection [of parts].
Formed here and there,
long nurtured for a long time—
this is the state of views for one who does not know.
Those who do not know speak to us thus:
"One is a brahmin by birth.
But one does not become a brahmin by birth.
One does not become a non-Brahmin by birth;
by one’s deeds one becomes a Brahmin,
and by one’s deeds one becomes a non-Brahmin.
By action one is a farmer,
by action one is a craftsman;
by action one is a merchant.
One becomes a physician by means of action;
one becomes a thief by means of action,
and a professional warrior by means of action.
One becomes a sacrificer through action;
one also becomes a king through action.
Thus is this, according to reality.
The wise perceive karma;
seeing dependent origination,
they are skilled in the ripening of karma.
By karma the world revolves,
by karma the generation revolves;
beings are bound by karma.
Like the linchpin of a moving chariot,
[one is held fast] by austerity, the holy life,
self-restraint, and self-control.
By this one becomes a brahmin;
this is the supreme brahminhood.
One endowed with the threefold knowledge,
The noble ones have exhausted rebirth;
know this, Vāseṭṭha,
regarding Brahmā and Sakka, for those who understand.
When this was said, the young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or as one might show the way to one who has lost their path, or as one might hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Gotama in many ways.
We go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The Vāseṭṭha Sutta, the eighth, is finished.
